unit_label: Module C unit 2 (courseware unit 18), part 1: financial statements, users, concepts, balance sheet and profit and loss formats, cash flow and funds flow

facts.statement: Whenever a bank considers a loan proposal, it needs the financial details of the prospective as well as the existing borrower; financial statements are the backbone of any credit proposal and the premise of any credit decision. They are the formal records of the financial activities of a business, give an overview of its financial condition in the short, medium and long term, and are used to assess overall position and operating results. Ratio analysis shows whether the business is improving or deteriorating over past years and allows comparison among entities. Analysis helps determine liquidity position, long term solvency, financial viability and profitability.

The Companies Act, 2013 (section 2(40)) defines financial statements as a set of: a balance sheet as at the end of the financial year; a profit and loss account (or income and expenditure account for a company carrying on an activity not for profit); a cash flow statement; a statement of changes in equity, if applicable; and any explanatory note annexed to or forming part of these documents. The financial statements of a one person company, small company, dormant company and start-up company may not include the cash flow statement. Where a company has one or more subsidiaries, associate companies or joint ventures, section 129(3) requires a consolidated financial statement of the company and all of them in the same form and manner as its own.
facts.locator: S01 printed p. 424 (statutory statement, courseware account, not checked against the Act)

facts.statement: Financial statements are prepared for the use of several stakeholders: lenders, creditors, investors, government departments and agencies, rating agencies, customers, employees, the general public and analysts. They are prepared by management and audited; the auditor only gives an opinion, so lenders analyse them for themselves. On receiving audited financials the credit officer should check their genuineness and verify them at fresh sanction, renewal or review, with those available on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs website; where the audited financials are not available there, an independent confirmation should be obtained from the Chartered Accountant firm and recorded in the proposal; major items of the profit and loss account and balance sheet should be cross-checked with the statutory and regulatory returns. The statements must be read together with the auditor's report and its notes.

The Directors' Report gives financial results highlights, the future plan of the company, the dividend, the directors' responsibility statement, the accounting standards followed, the true and fair view of the financial statements, proper maintenance of books and safeguards for assets and against fraud, going concern, adequate internal financial control and compliance with applicable laws. The auditor's report is the auditor's opinion, based on the audit, on the true and fair representation of the material facts in the financial statements, and the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 is the statutory format in which the auditor reports on other legal and regulatory requirements.

The basic concepts used in preparing financial statements named by the courseware are: accrual, consistency, going concern, prudence, separate entity, money measurement, stable monetary unit, cost, conservatism, dual aspect, accounting period, realisation, matching and full disclosure.

Accounting Standards are written policy documents covering recognition, measurement, classification, presentation and disclosure of accounting transactions and events; their objective is to reduce the alternatives in preparing financial statements within the bounds of rationality, ensure comparability of the statements of different enterprises and provide meaningful information to users. Accounting Standards were formulated by the Accounting Standards Board constituted by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India; International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) are accounting standards developed by the International Accounting Standards Board; India adapted them as Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), which differ from IFRS to suit the Indian economic and legal environment. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India recommends standards to the National Financial Reporting Authority, and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs notifies them. If a provision of an applicable Act conflicts with an Ind AS, the provision of the Act prevails to that extent.

The Companies Act 2013 prescribes the formats of the balance sheet and profit and loss account (Schedule III), except for insurance, banking and electricity companies and companies governed by any other law, which have formats under their own laws. The financial statements must give a true and fair view of the state of affairs, comply with the accounting standards, and, where they do not, disclose the deviation, the reasons and any financial effects. The accounting year is the period ending on 31 March (with exceptions, such as a company incorporated on or after 1 January, whose first period ends on 31 March of the following year); every company must prepare financial statements even if there is no activity or the project is not completed.

A balance sheet is a statement of assets (what is owned) and liabilities (what is owed to others) at a particular moment, like a snapshot, and must show the date as at which it is prepared. An asset is classified as current if it is expected to be realised in, or intended for sale or consumption in, the normal operating cycle; if it is held primarily for trading; if it is expected to be realised within twelve months after the reporting date; or if it is cash or cash equivalent unless restricted from exchange or from settling a liability for at least twelve months after the reporting date; all other assets are non-current. A liability is current if it is expected to be settled in the normal operating cycle; if it is held primarily for trading; if it is due to be settled within twelve months after the reporting date; or if the company has no unconditional right to defer settlement for at least twelve months after the reporting date; all other liabilities are non-current. A receivable is a trade receivable if it is due on account of goods sold or services rendered in the normal course of business, and a payable is a trade payable if it is due on account of goods purchased or services received in the normal course of business.
facts.locator: S01 printed p. 430 (general instructions of Schedule III as given by the courseware)

facts.statement: In the Schedule III format, the equity and liabilities side shows shareholders' funds (share capital, reserves and surplus, money received against share warrants), share application money pending allotment, non-current liabilities (long-term borrowings, deferred tax liabilities (net), other long-term liabilities, long-term provisions) and current liabilities (short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities, short-term provisions). The assets side shows non-current assets (fixed assets: tangible, intangible, capital work-in-progress and intangible assets under development; non-current investments; deferred tax assets (net); long-term loans and advances; other non-current assets) and current assets (current investments, inventories, trade receivables, cash and cash equivalents, short-term loans and advances, other current assets). Notes disclose, among other things, the classes and amounts of share capital; the split of borrowings into secured and unsecured; trade receivables outstanding for more than six months from the due date; the classes of inventory including goods in transit; and contingent liabilities (claims against the company not acknowledged as debt, guarantees, other money for which the company is contingently liable) and commitments.

In the Schedule III statement of profit and loss, revenue from operations plus other income gives total revenue; expenses (cost of materials consumed, purchases of stock-in-trade, changes in inventories, employee benefit expense, finance costs, depreciation and amortisation and other expenses) are deducted to arrive at profit before exceptional and extraordinary items and tax; exceptional items and extraordinary items are then adjusted to reach profit before tax; tax expense (current tax and deferred tax) is deducted to give profit from continuing operations; profit or loss from discontinuing operations (after tax) is added to give the profit or loss for the period; and earnings per equity share are shown both basic and diluted. Finance costs are classified as interest expense, other borrowing costs and net gain or loss on foreign currency transactions and translation. Other income is classified as interest income (for a company other than a finance company), dividend income, net gain or loss on sale of investments and other non-operating income. For a company other than a finance company revenue from operations is shown by sale of products, sale of services and other operating revenues, less excise duty; for a finance company it includes revenue from interest and other financial services.

A cash flow statement shows the movement of cash and cash equivalents, into or out of a business during a period: it starts with the opening cash balance in the first balance sheet, adds the sources of cash and deducts the uses, to arrive at the closing balance, which must equal the cash shown in the second balance sheet. Cash comprises cash on hand and demand deposits with banks; cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into cash at any time without any significant erosion in value. The three components are operating cash flows (cash received or spent in the course of business operations, which should be positive for the company to remain solvent), investment cash flows (cash receipts and payments of a long-term nature other than for or from operations, which exclude capital and debt transactions) and financing cash flows (cash transactions relating to capital and debt). Uses include checking whether profit and net cash flow are aligned, whether the income recognised on the accrual basis is acceptable, and the ability to meet sure and timely cash outflows such as repayment of an ad hoc loan or retirement of a usance letter of credit.

A funds flow statement treats each balance sheet item as a source or a use of funds: when two balance sheets are compared, an increase in a liability or a decrease in an asset (other than cash) is an additional source of funds, and an increase in an asset or a decrease in a liability is an additional use of funds. The statement between two balance sheet dates shows what happened to the excess of long term sources over long term uses, that is, to the Net Working Capital; if more long term uses were made than long term sources, net working capital falls, denoting diversion.

payload.title: The basic accounting concepts
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware names fourteen concepts behind the statements:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Accrual** | **Consistency** | **Going concern** |
| **Prudence** | **Separate entity** | **Money measurement** |
| **Stable monetary unit** | **Cost** | **Conservatism** |
| **Dual aspect** | **Accounting period** | **Realisation** |
| **Matching** | **Full disclosure** | |

In plain terms for a banker: **accrual** counts income and expense when earned or incurred, not when cash moves; **going concern** assumes the business continues; **prudence** avoids overstating profit; **matching** sets expenses against the income they helped earn; **consistency** keeps methods the same from year to year.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The plain-terms line is an editorial gloss; the courseware only lists the names.

payload.title: Accounting standards, Ind AS and the form of the statements
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Accounting standards** set out how to **recognise, measure, classify, present and disclose** transactions. Their aim is to **reduce alternatives**, give **comparability** between enterprises and give users **meaningful information**.

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Accounting Standards Board** (set up by ICAI) | Formulated the Accounting Standards |
| **IASB** | Develops **IFRS** |
| **ICAI** | Recommends standards to the **NFRA** |
| **Ministry of Corporate Affairs** | **Notifies** the standards |

**Ind AS** is India's adaptation of IFRS, changed to fit the Indian economic and legal setting. If an **Act conflicts** with an Ind AS, the **Act prevails**.

**Form (courseware account):** formats of the balance sheet and profit and loss account are in the Act, except for **insurance, banking, electricity** and companies under other laws. The statements must give a **true and fair view**, comply with the standards and **disclose any deviation**, its reasons and financial effect. The accounting year ends on **31 March**, and every company must prepare statements **even if there is no activity**.

payload.title: Balance sheet: current and non-current
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **balance sheet** is a **snapshot** of what the entity **owns (assets)** and **owes (liabilities)** at a date, which it must state.

| | **Current** if | Otherwise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Asset** | Realised, sold or consumed in the **normal operating cycle**; or **held for trading**; or realised **within 12 months** after the reporting date; or **cash or cash equivalent** (unless restricted for at least 12 months) | **Non-current** |
| **Liability** | Settled in the **normal operating cycle**; or **held for trading**; or due **within 12 months**; or the company has **no unconditional right to defer** settlement for 12 months | **Non-current** |

A **trade receivable** is due for **goods sold or services rendered in the normal course of business**; a **trade payable** is due for **goods or services bought** in the normal course.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Current versus non-current drives the liquidity ratios you will use later.

self_check.prompt_text: A loan due for repayment in nine months. Current or non-current?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Current, because it is due within twelve months of the reporting date.

payload.title: The balance sheet format
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Equity and liabilities**

1. **Shareholders' funds:** share capital; reserves and surplus; money against share warrants
2. **Share application money pending allotment**
3. **Non-current liabilities:** long-term borrowings; deferred tax liabilities (net); other long-term liabilities; long-term provisions
4. **Current liabilities:** short-term borrowings; trade payables; other current liabilities; short-term provisions

**Assets**

1. **Non-current assets:** fixed assets (tangible, intangible, capital work-in-progress, intangible assets under development); non-current investments; deferred tax assets (net); long-term loans and advances; other non-current assets
2. **Current assets:** current investments; inventories; trade receivables; cash and cash equivalents; short-term loans and advances; other current assets

**Notes worth a banker's attention:** secured versus unsecured **borrowings**; trade receivables **outstanding more than six months**; **goods in transit** within inventories; **contingent liabilities** (claims not acknowledged as debt, guarantees, other) and **commitments**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Contingent liabilities are not on the balance sheet total but may become real obligations.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which head do trade payables appear?

payload.title: The statement of profit and loss
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Step | Item |
| --- | --- |
| I | **Revenue from operations** |
| II | **Other income** |
| III | **Total revenue** = I + II |
| IV | **Expenses:** materials consumed, purchases of stock-in-trade, changes in inventories, employee benefits, **finance costs**, **depreciation and amortisation**, other expenses |
| V | **Profit before exceptional and extraordinary items and tax** = III - IV |
| | Adjust for **exceptional** and **extraordinary** items to get **profit before tax** |
| | Deduct **tax** (current and deferred) to get **profit from continuing operations** |
| | Add **discontinuing operations** (after tax) to get **profit for the period** |
| | **Earnings per share:** **basic** and **diluted** |

**Finance costs:** interest expense, other borrowing costs, net foreign exchange gain or loss.

**Other income:** interest income (non-finance company), dividend income, net gain or loss on sale of investments, other non-operating income.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The extraordinary items line follows the courseware format; check the current Schedule III for its use.

self_check.prompt_text: What is total revenue in this format?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Revenue from operations plus other income.

payload.title: The cash flow statement
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **cash flow statement (CFS)** follows **cash and cash equivalents** over the period:

**Opening cash + sources of cash - uses of cash = Closing cash**, which must equal the cash in the second balance sheet.

**Cash** = cash on hand and **demand deposits** with banks. **Cash equivalents** = **short-term, highly liquid** investments readily convertible into cash **without significant erosion in value**.

| Component | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Operating** | Cash from and for running the business; should be **positive** for the company to **stay solvent** |
| **Investment** | **Long-term** receipts and payments not from operations (capital and debt transactions excluded) |
| **Financing** | Transactions in **capital and debt** |

**What the lender learns:** whether **profit and net cash flow agree**, whether accrual income is **actually turning into cash**, and whether the business can meet **sure, timely outflows** such as an ad hoc loan repayment or retiring a usance letter of credit.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A profitable company can still run out of cash; the CFS shows that.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of the three cash flows should be positive for the company to remain solvent?

payload.title: Closing cash from the three flows
payload.core_explanation_md: A firm's opening cash is Rs 40 lakh. During the year operating cash flow is +Rs 95 lakh, investment cash flow is -Rs 70 lakh and financing cash flow is +Rs 25 lakh. Find the closing cash.

worked_steps.description: Add the three flows to get the net movement.
Add the net movement to the opening cash.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Closing cash Rs 90 lakh, which must match the cash in the later balance sheet

self_check.prompt_text: If the later balance sheet shows Rs 85 lakh, what does that tell you?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Something has been left out or misclassified in the statement; it should be Rs 90 lakh.

payload.title: The funds flow statement
payload.core_explanation_md:
Compare **two balance sheets**. Each change in an item (other than cash) is a **source** or a **use** of funds:

| Change | Source or use |
| --- | --- |
| **Increase** in a **liability** | **Source** |
| **Decrease** in an **asset** | **Source** |
| **Increase** in an **asset** | **Use** |
| **Decrease** in a **liability** | **Use** |

The statement traces the surplus of **long term sources over long term uses**, in other words what became of **net working capital**. If **more is used long term than raised long term**, net working capital **falls**: the funds have been **diverted** (for example, short term money financing long term assets).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Net working capital = current assets less current liabilities.

self_check.prompt_text: A company raises a new term loan. Source or use?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A source, because a liability has increased.

payload.title: Sources and uses of funds and the change in net working capital
payload.core_explanation_md: Between two balance sheets a firm issued shares of Rs 50 lakh, retained profit of Rs 60 lakh, added back depreciation of Rs 30 lakh, bought machinery for Rs 90 lakh and repaid a term loan of Rs 20 lakh. Find the effect on net working capital.

worked_steps.description: Sources minus uses is the change in net working capital.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Net working capital increases by Rs 30 lakh

self_check.prompt_text: If the machinery had cost Rs 150 lakh, what would happen?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Uses of Rs 170 lakh would exceed sources of Rs 140 lakh and net working capital would fall by Rs 30 lakh.
